title: Hang a picture
intro: A straight picture at the right height, with a hook and pin or adhesive strips if you rent.

steps.t: Mark the centre of the picture at [[145-150 cm]] from the floor. Over a sofa, the bottom edge goes [[20-25 cm]] above the back.
Measure the picture's height and mark the top edge: half the height above the centre mark.
On the back, pull the wire up taut and measure how far it sits below the top edge: mark the nail that far below the top mark.
Choose the fixing: hook and pin for plaster and brick, a plasterboard hook, or adhesive strips if you can't drill.
With a hook: hold it on the mark and tap the angled pin in gently until the hook sits tight against the wall.
steps.q: Is the hook firm when you tug it?
steps.fix: If the pin goes in with no grip or the wall crumbles, use a plug and screw or a plasterboard hook.

steps.t: With strips: clean the wall and the back of the frame with alcohol, then let it dry for a minute.
Stick the strips to the frame, press the picture on the mark, take it off and press each strip on the wall for 30 seconds.
Wait an hour before putting the picture back on the strips: the adhesive needs to bond.
steps.label: Bonding

steps.t: Hang the picture on the hook, or clip it back onto the strips, pressing firmly.
Put the level on the top edge and straighten the picture until the bubble is centred.
steps.q: Is the picture straight, with the bubble centred?
steps.fix: On a wire, slide it along the hook; with strips, unclip it and press it back on straight.

tips: Cut a paper template the size of the frame and tape it up first: you'll see at once if the height works.
Pictures over [[5 kg]]: skip the strips and use two hooks or a plug and screw.
Hanging a group? Treat it as one block and put the centre of the group at [[145-150 cm]].

title: Fill a hole or crack in a wall
intro: Plug holes, cracks or dents in plaster or plasterboard: a smooth wall ready to paint.

steps.t: Remove screws and wall plugs, then scrape out anything crumbly with the knife. Open cracks into a slight V.
Brush the dust out and dampen the edges lightly with a wrung-out sponge: the filler grips better.
Press filler into the hole with the filling knife, criss-cross, leaving it slightly proud of the wall.
Let it dry: the filler is ready when it has turned evenly pale, centre included.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Filler shrinks as it dries: spread a thin second coat, wider than the hole, feathering it out at the edges.
Let the second coat dry. Deep holes take longer: press the centre, it should feel hard.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Sand with light circular strokes until you can't feel a ridge between filler and wall when you run your hand over it.
steps.q: Is the filler flush with the wall, smooth and with no dip?
steps.fix: If there's still a dip, add a very thin skim and let it dry; if it sticks out, sand some more.

steps.t: Wipe off all the dust with a barely damp cloth and wait until the surface is dry again.
Prime the filled patch, going a little beyond it: otherwise a dull patch will show through the paint.

tips: Holes deeper than [[1 cm]]: fill in thin layers and let each one dry before the next.
In plasterboard, holes over [[5 cm]] need a patch first: self-adhesive mesh or a piece of board, then filler.
If a crack keeps reopening or getting wider, the building may be moving: have a surveyor look at it.

title: Remove mould from a wall
intro: Black spots in corners or behind furniture: remove them and protect the wall so they stay away.

steps.t: Open the window wide and keep children and pets out of the room. Put on gloves, mask and glasses.
Pull the furniture away from the wall and cover the floor under the patch with the dust sheet.
Spray the mould remover over the whole patch and [[20 cm]] around it; don't scrub it dry. Or use bleach, 1 part to 4 of water.
steps.w: Never mix bleach with limescale removers, vinegar or ammonia: it releases toxic gas.

steps.t: Leave it for the time on the label, usually 15 minutes. Stay out of the room or near the open window.
steps.label: Contact time

steps.t: Wipe with the damp sponge from the edges inwards, rinsing it often. Bin the sponge when you're done.
Look at the wall in good light: the black spots should be gone or much lighter.
steps.fix: Spray again, leave it and wipe again. If grey shadows stay in the plaster, the anti-mould paint will cover them.

steps.t: Let the wall dry completely with air moving through the room: usually about a day.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Roll on the first coat of anti-mould paint, brushing into the corners and going beyond the treated area.
Let the first coat dry as the tin says, with the window ajar.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Apply the second coat of anti-mould paint evenly, with no bare patches.
Put the hygrometer in the room and check the humidity over the next few days, especially in the morning.
steps.q: Does the humidity stay between 40 and 60%?
steps.fix: Air the room 10 minutes a day, use the extractor fans, move furniture off the wall; if needed, get a dehumidifier.

tips: Mould that keeps coming back in the same spot, or a wall that's damp to the touch, may mean a leak: call a pro.
If wallpaper or plasterboard is soaked through, the mould is inside: that piece has to be cut out and replaced.
Keep wardrobes and sofas [[5-10 cm]] off outside walls: air moving behind them prevents condensation.

title: Put up a wall shelf
intro: Fix a level, solid shelf, with the right drill bit and wall plug for your type of wall.

mats.n: Wall plugs to suit the wall

steps.t: Knock on the wall: a hollow sound means plasterboard; solid means brick or concrete. Hollow brick shows when you drill.
Run the detector over where you'll drill. Avoid the vertical and horizontal lines running from sockets and switches.
steps.q: Does the detector show no pipes, cables or metal in that area?
steps.fix: Move the shelf a few centimetres and check again. If in doubt, don't drill there.
steps.w: Never drill straight above or below sockets and switches: that's where cables usually run.

steps.t: Choose the height, mark the first hole in pencil and hold the bracket against the mark.
Put the level on the shelf or between the brackets and mark all the holes, with the bubble dead centre.
steps.q: Is the line between the marks level?
steps.fix: Rub out and re-mark from the first hole; the bubble must sit exactly between the two lines.

steps.t: Fit a masonry bit the same size as the plug, usually [[6 mm]] or [[8 mm]]. Hammer mode only on concrete and solid brick.
Mark the depth on the bit with tape (plug length + [[5 mm]]) and drill straight in without forcing it.
steps.w: Hold the drill with both hands and keep your glasses on: dust and chips fly out.

steps.t: Vacuum or blow the dust out of the hole: a clean hole makes the plug hold much better.
Push in the right plug: standard for solid walls, long for hollow brick, metal cavity or spring toggle for plasterboard.
Screw the brackets into the plugs; tighten until firm but no more, or the plug will spin.
Rest the shelf on the brackets, put the level on top and push down on it with your hand.
steps.q: Is the shelf level and solid when you push it?
steps.fix: If a plug spins or pulls out, use a bigger or chemical anchor; if it's crooked, redrill a little to one side.

steps.t: Screw the shelf to the brackets from underneath with short screws that won't come through the top.

tips: On plasterboard, for heavy loads screw into the metal studs or use rated anchors: check the load on the pack.
To keep it clean, tape an open paper envelope under the hole: it catches the dust.
If water comes out or the bit hits metal, stop at once: shut off the water or power and call a pro.

title: Paint a wall
intro: Refresh a wall or change its colour with an even finish, no patchy areas and clean edges.

steps.t: Move the furniture to the middle of the room and lay the dust sheet along the wall, taping it down.
Tape the skirting or baseboards, frames, sockets and the ceiling edge; press the tape down firmly with a fingernail.
Fill holes and cracks, sand once the filler is dry, then dust the wall down with a soft broom.
New plaster, stains or a chalky surface? Apply primer and let it dry. Otherwise skip this step.
steps.label: Primer

steps.t: Stir the paint well from the bottom. Thin it with water as the tin says, usually a bit more for the first coat.
With the brush, cut in a strip about [[5 cm]] wide along the tape, in the corners and under the ceiling.
steps.w: On the ladder, don't lean out sideways: climb down and move it. Keep off the top two steps.

steps.t: Load the roller, roll off the excess on the tray and paint a W in patches of about [[1 m2]], then fill in without lifting off.
Lay off each patch top to bottom with a nearly dry roller, in parallel strokes that overlap slightly.
steps.q: Is the paint on with no runs or drips?
steps.fix: Roll over them straight away with a dry roller while wet; if a skin has formed, let it dry and sand.

steps.t: Let the first coat dry with a window ajar: it should be dry to the touch and even in colour.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Second coat: cut in the edges with the brush first, then roll in a W, laying off top to bottom.
Look along the wall at an angle, towards the window light, for pale patches or streaks.
steps.q: Is the colour even, with no pale areas or roller marks?
steps.fix: Touch up pale spots with a nearly dry roller; if it's patchy all over, add a third coat once dry.

steps.t: Pull the tape off now, while the paint is still wet: slowly, at an angle away from the paint.

tips: Don't paint below [[10 °C]] or with direct sun on the wall: the paint dries badly and shows marks.
Taking a break? Wrap the roller and brush in a plastic bag: they stay wet for hours.
Always finish a whole wall without stopping halfway: the join would show.
